title: Palliative sedation and controlled sedation for refractory suffering

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source decision-language and institution-gate synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no individual advice, no legal or clinical determination.
limitations: Public sources support vocabulary and broad decision-context orientation only; they do not supply consented bedside testimony.
This record must not become clinical, legal, emergency, eligibility, medication, or procedural advice.
Local law, institutional policy, care team guidance, and the person’s documented wishes govern actual decisions.

moment.plain_scene: When symptoms remain severe despite other efforts, a team may discuss sedation to reduce awareness and suffering; families may confuse this with euthanasia, ordinary drowsiness, sleep, or abandonment.
ordinary_language_queries: is palliative sedation the same as euthanasia

content_layers.observation_text: This record holds a dangerous vocabulary boundary: sedation may be a legitimate professional response to refractory suffering, but the public page must not become a medication pathway or a metaphysical argument.
content_layers.source_synthesis: PCNOW describes controlled sedation for refractory suffering as sedation for intractable distress in the dying; the EAPC framework is professional guidance for healthcare professionals; NICE last-days guidance supports individualized symptom assessment and specialist advice when symptoms do not improve or undesirable sedation occurs.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: Decision-language records should preserve how the term enters the room, what ordinary readers might think it means, and what must be routed back to trained/local authority.

what_this_is_not: not MAID/euthanasia equivalence or distinction adjudication for every jurisdiction
not proof that a person was or was not suffering
uncertainties: Terms vary by country, state/province, institution, and clinical context.
The same word can be used differently by clinicians, families, forms, and media.
Public sources do not capture the full emotional, cultural, disability, language-access, or family-conflict context.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should define the term only enough to reduce panic and confusion, then direct all specifics to the care team.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should capture symptom refractoriness, proportionality language, consent/surrogate process, family explanation, and distinction from ordinary medication side effects.
language_notes: Render the term as room-language first, not as a command.
Preserve uncertainty and jurisdictional limits before definitions.
Avoid euphemisms that obscure consent, capacity, rights, or clinical scope.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the decision-language and institution-gate layer. It requires domain review before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not legal advice, not eligibility screening, not a medication or procedure instruction, not a prognosis, not a ritual authority, and not a substitute for the person’s care team, emergency services, legal counsel, ethics committee, organ procurement process, or local law.
